extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of journalism interested in Joseph Pulitzer and journalistic standards
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and implied hiring/evaluation criteria for people who will write for or serve a mass-circulation newspaper (specifically The World) and for staff working closely with a powerful, blind publisher. Emphasizes style, accuracy, memory, preparation, and personal qualities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Candidate personal qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Must have tact, patience, a sense of humor, the gift of condensing information, and, above all, a respect, a love, a passion for accuracy. (Pulitzer: "I must explore your brain, your character, your tastes, your sympathies, your prejudices, your temper; I must find out if you have tact, patience, a sense of humor, the gift of condensing information, and, above all, a respect, a love, a passion for accuracy.")
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pulitzer tests candidates personally (drives, conversation, reading) to ascertain these traits. The surrounding text emphasizes emotional steadiness, tact, discretions, and the ability to condense and present material accurately to him and to a mass audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing characteristics for The World
rubrics_metrics.description: The American people want something terse, forcible, picturesque, striking — something that will arrest their attention, enlist their sympathy, arouse their indignation, stimulate their imagination, convince their reason, awaken their conscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pulitzer insists copy must be brief so people will read it, clear so they will understand it, forcible so they will appreciate it, picturesque so they will remember it, and above all accurate so they may be wisely guided by it. Writing for The World differs from writing for more narrowly educated papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial responsibility to readers
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the duty of the paper to see that readers 'get the truth' and to present it so that a mass audience may be wisely guided by its light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because The World reaches about a million readers a day, the editor/writer has a responsibility to accuracy and conscience; truth without accuracy or suitable presentation is inadequate for such an audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memory as a valued faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulitzer regarded memory as 'the highest faculty of the human mind' and expected staff to have tenacious memories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text gives examples (committing lists of names and figures to memory to impress J.P.). Memory is tested in conversation and used as evidence of capacity to condense and recall material for immediate use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Morning reading preferences (content selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: During the breakfast hour J. P. would not have anything read to him which was of an exciting nature — this preference excluded political news, crime, disaster, and war correspondence and left practically nothing but book reviews, criticisms of plays, operas, and art exhibitions, and publishers' announcements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selectors preparing reading material should favor literary and cultural pieces for the breakfast period; avoid sensational or highly emotive reports at that time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation of material ('prepared')
rubrics_metrics.description: To 'prepare' material means to read it rapidly once and then go over it again with concentration so that the more important articles can be marked for actual reading, the other portions being dealt with conversationally; everything being boiled down to its essence before it reached Mr. Pulitzer's ear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit workflow requirement for secretaries/readers: triage large amounts of press copy, mark what to read aloud, and condense or conversationalize the remainder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive minuteness for a blind principal
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked to describe a scene for the blind publisher, one must 'never think that anything is too small or insignificant to be of interest' and 'describe everything with the greatest minuteness, every cloud in the sky, every shadow on the hillside, every tree, every house, every dress, every wrinkle on a face, everything, everything.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For someone reading/describing sensory detail to a blind person, exhaustive, precise, and minute description is required; nothing should be assumed unimportant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation in humor and entertainment
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid being too funny or too dull; Mr. Pulitzer needed neither extremes—too dull offended his sensitiveness, too funny caused physical pain from excessive laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When entertaining or presenting material, strike a balance: provide humor but avoid causing excessive physical exertion or dullness; tailor entertainment to the principal's sensitivities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing by manufactured difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Pulitzer's fixed policy was to make things as complicated and difficult as possible for a candidate in order quickly to discover whether a new man would suit him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes a hiring/evaluation method: induce situations that provoke impatience, bad temper, or poor tact; candidates who remain patient and good-humored advance to further tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major-domo (house manager) capabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The major-domo must be capable and efficient in the highest degree; duties ranged from nursing to diplomacy, producing hot-water bottles, arranging special trains, collecting newspapers from remote places, procuring out-of-season food, and monopolizing services of administrations when required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The role requires resourcefulness, speed, discretion, diplomatic influence, and the ability to both execute and undo complex arrangements at the master's whim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptability of prior experience to new audience
rubrics_metrics.description: You mustn't think that because you've written articles for the London Times you are competent to write for The World. It's a very different matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience at one paper or for an educated, smaller readership does not automatically qualify a writer for a mass-circulation paper; writers must adapt style (brevity, force, picturesqueness, accuracy) to the new audience.
